utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. May we hear the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is case number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, please for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, Ann Sutherland, assisted by Ruth Karper, case manager. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic, John Ostojic and Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: One of the few good news of this morning is that the witness is ready and without any further ado, please let's start. In the meantime, I may announce that in all likelihood, Mr. Peter Stanar will testify next Monday. Mr. Kuruzovic either already on Tuesday or on Wednesday next week. As we said yesterday, this would be during the rebuttal period of time with the agreement of the parties. Later on, I'll ask the Prosecution whether or not the Prosecution intends to call the now-available Mr. Dosen during rebuttal but not now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Trifkovic. I hope you feel better now as well and you're fit for the continuation of your expert testimony today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour, yes, I feel much better than I did over the past couple of days even though I'm not back 100 per cent in top form but I think I'm up to it for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: That's what we have in common. The Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Trifkovic.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Today, we are in full force and because I was questioning you on Friday, I'll continue, although Mr. Ostojic is with us as well. On Friday we finished with your opinion on the role of Dr. Stakic before the 30th of April, 1992, and now I would like to ask you, based upon review of the documents provided, as Donia's report, numerous articles and literature, my other things, can you please describe for us Dr. Stakic's role after the takeover of Prijedor municipality on April the 30th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not want to interrupt but I wonder if in the light of this question, the witness could indicate on what he's basing this answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Certainly, the witness will do, and refer to concrete parts of articles that we have the necessary basis for this. The more concrete we are, the better it is, no doubt, you know Dr. Trifkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Your Honour. My only basis for forming an opinion in this respect, the published sources, specifically the Kozarski Vjesnik newspaper, which seems to have carried fairly faithfully public pronouncements of different officials, both before and after the events of May of 1992. As I indicated in my examination-in-chief on Friday afternoon, prior to the events of the spring of 1992, Dr. Stakic acted, if anything, more like a Yugo nostalgist than a greater Serb nationalist and the tone of one might say conciliatory regret over the way that events were shaping up is also strongly felt in his interview entitled -- under the headline, "Serbs live in this municipality too." That was published in February of 1992 in Kozarski Vjesnik. In that interview, Stakic elaborated at some length on the reasons for the establishment of the Serb municipality in Prijedor, pointing out the desire of the SDA to marginalise the SDS and present it with faits accomplis and also stressing the need to have functioning organs in the municipality and to overcome the blockade of its organs by the central ministries in Sarajevo. In the period after the spring of 1992, I think that particularly poignant is the interview or rather sorry the report that we had on the occasion of the bishop -- of Bishop Komarica's visit to Prijedor. He's the Roman Catholic bishop of Banja Luka. I'm now speaking from memory. I can of course verify the specific dates if need be but for the sake of the narrative I think it's easier. When bishop Komarica came to Banja Luka, accompanied by both his -- some of his priests and HDZ officials, Dr. Stakic spoke in terms again of ethnic conciliation, of the need for rebuilding trust and rebuilding connections that will endure even after the war is over. When he appealed on the Ukrainians in the Prijedor municipality to remain in their homes, there is a small Ukrainian or Ruthenian community in the Prijedor municipality, they were settled there in the 19th century by the Austrians. He also spoke in terms of the need to overcome the legacy of ethnic divisions and of the need to create conditions for common co-living "suzivot" is I think the term used, and all of this indicates that even if indeed it was his agenda to seek a radical nationalist solution to the situation in the Prijedor municipality, he chose a very unusual method of pursuing that objective, because elsewhere, in the former Yugoslavia, and I'm talking about all sides of the ethnic divide, it was common practice for people of strongly nationalist persuasion to use the language of threats, vilification, even demonisation of other ethnic groups. I stress again this was practice common to Serbs, as well as Croats, as well as Muslims, and the process of eventual ethnic cleansing, whether it be the Muslims in Foca or the Serbs in Mostar or the Croats in Central Bosnia was almost invariably preceded by a campaign of verbal abuse and a torrent of hate speech that had the objective of encouraging people to leave of their own volition even before the violence started in earnest. It is my considered opinion that the public announcements of Dr. Stakic did not fit that pattern.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Dr. Trifkovic, would you be so kind and look at your list of documents, the shorter one? I'll try to point out a few numbers so you can tell us whether those documents are among others you considered when testifying about the -- Dr. Stakic's personality and conduct. It's number 018, 022, 048, 054, 059, 064, 067, and 073.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have to emphasise that you're now referring also to several documents that we've dealt with in -- on Friday afternoon. I didn't specifically refer to them now because I thought the question referred specifically to the period after the takeover of the Assembly. Of course, the documents that you list now also refer to the period leading up to the rupture, specifically Stakic's speech at the November 29th celebration in 1991, which I dealt with on Friday and which I characterised as an example of what I would term Yugo nostalgic rather than greater Serb discourse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Maybe it's my own fault but asking my colleagues, we are not aware of this what you call short list. Could you please, for a better understanding of that, what the expert tells us, provide us with the short list? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Dr. Trifkovic, do you have an opinion, based upon a reasonable degree of certainty, of other comparable conflicts in history?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, the list is long and very sad. I didn't expect this question but if you give me just a moment to try and focus, I will certainly try to give you an answer. Without going into ancient history, if you simply look at the modern period from the end of Napoleonic wars from 1815 onwards, it is unfortunate that in European conflicts, there had been an increasing tendency to turn disputes over power and territory into all-national disputes in which the civilians were both the stake and the chief victims. The shifting ethnic picture, as the result of those conflicts roughly runs as follows: There was a shift in the ethnic composition of Schleswig-Holstein in the aftermath of Denmark's defeat at the hands of Prussia in 1864. There was an attempt by the second Reich to alter the ethnic picture of Alsace and Lorraine through loyalty oaths in the period of 1871 to 1914. There was the exodus of the Turks from the Ottoman Empire's Balkan possessions in the aftermath of the Balkan wars of 1912. There was an ethnic shift in the newly acquired Polish parts of Silesia and Pomerania in 1919, and so on. But the most drastic examples of the ethnic balance being altered by the force of arms came in 1945, when, with the advance of the Red Army, the Poles who had lived east of the Curzon line roughly the Bug River were forced west into what used to be called the little Poland or the Duchy of Warsaw, while the Germans who had lived east of the Oder-Neisse line in the Asian provinces of east Prussia, Pomerania and Silesia, were even though it's maybe politically incorrect to say so in the context, but, yes, they were ethnically cleansed and forced west of those two rivers. The same fate befell the Sudeten Germans in Czechoslovakia and the Volksdeutscher in Yugoslavia. Further instances of ethnic cleansing of effectively innocent civilians is the consequence of World War II, affected the Italians in Istria and maritime Slovenia. The Germans of Bessarabia and to a lesser extent the Tyrolese south of the Brenner Pass and Alto Adige. The total number of persons thus affected is estimated variously between 12 and 15 million. Outside Europe, the most drastic example of the change of ethnic composition resulting from war or civil war was in the Indian subcontinent where, in the period 1947-48, in addition to millions of people slaughtered, an effective, although chaotic exchange of population had taken place resulting in the creation of the state of Pakistan, the Muslim state of Pakistan, and the exodus of Hindus both from east Pakistan, today's Bangladesh, and from Bihar [phoen], today's Pakistan proper. In addition, I forgot to mention in the aftermath of World War I, the ethnic cleansing and population exchange between Greece and Turkey where long-established Greek settlements along the Aegean coast of Asia Minor, numbering 2 million people and centred on the city of Smyrna, today's Izmir, were wiped out and likewise, the long-established Turkish communities in Greece, both in the islands and on the mainland were expelled. So one may say that over the past 100 years, we have witnessed a number of instances where disputes over land, over territory, and power, were inexorably linked with the process that over the past decade has come to be known as ethnic cleansing. I have little doubt in my mind that similar fate would have befallen the unionists of Northern Ireland, the Protestants, had there not been partition of the six counts of Ulster that were left under the British Crown in 1921. I'm afraid this is a sketchy answer to a serious question that merits more focused elaboration but not having been prepared for it, I've tried to give the best outline I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor. I would like to ask you now in your expert opinion, as an academic, historian and political scientist, how would you characterise the Bosnian and Herzegovinian conflict in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: I would start by stating what it was not. It was not a mysterious and irrational conflict springing from some ancient hatreds that go to the mists of pre-modern experience that is rooted in some atavistic blood lust of the savage Balkan peasants. In a funny way it was a rational conflict because it was a dispute over clearly defined objectives and I think what is often lost in the propagandistic discourse on the wars in the former Yugoslavia is the fact that each side has a relatively rational story to tell. The fact that this - and I use the term "rational" in strictly technical sense - the fact that this rational discourse is often lost is primarily due to the desire of different parties in the conflict to couch its interests in universal terms such as democracy, multi-culturalism, tolerance, and all the politically correct catch-all terms that are expected to be picked up by the rest of the world in the right kind of way. So let me try to give a succinct description of each side's position and expectations. With the disintegration of Yugoslavia, the Muslim side felt that it could claim the right of Bosnia-Herzegovina to independence on the same terms as those both claimed and obtained on January 15th, 1992, by Croatia and Slovenia. They did face a problem. The problem was the constitutional arrangements in Bosnia-Herzegovina that specifically precluded any change of constitutional status of the republic without the consensual agreement of all three constituent nations. The Muslim leadership tried to overcome this problem by forging a tactical alliance with the HDZ and by frankly pretending that the constitutional ban on two sides outvoting the third simply wasn't there. The Croat side was primarily interested in sooner or later joining in -- joining with Croatia but regarded the tactical step of forging a temporary alliance with the SDA for the purpose of detaching Bosnia-Herzegovina from Yugoslavia as a prudent and necessary first step in the process. The Serb side was determined not to be taken out of Yugoslavia by force and, in the extreme event of even accepting the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was determined not to allow the internal order of Bosnia-Herzegovina that would not give each constituent ethnic group the full degree of self-rule that would avoid a danger of majorisation or -- that's the Yugoslav term for the rule of one or a couple of ethnic groups over another -- and those three positions, incompatible as they seem, in terms of conflict management, could have been reconciled had there been on the part of the international community more of a technical skill in conflict resolution and conflict management. Since you ask about my opinion not only as a historian but also as a political scientist, I would say that in terms of games theory and in terms of the optimal model which would require for each side to give up some of its requirements but not to give up on its core requirement, probably the Cutilheiro Plan of February, 1992 or the Owen Stoltenberg tripartite federal plan of the fall of 1993 would provide the model that could have provided -- that could have avoided the worst aspects of the conflict. In other words, satisfying the Muslim core requirement for an internationally recognised and sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina with intact outside borders, and at the same time rearranging constitutional order of the republic in such a way as to allay the fears of Serbs and Croats of being marginalised by the most numerous ethnic group, and also giving expression to the fact already embodied in the pre-war Bosnian constitution, that the republic is constituted of three nations, three constituent ethnic groups, the consensus of which is required for any change of its constitutional status. So from purely technical point of view, the recognition of April 6th, 1992, even though ostensibly motivated by the desire to avoid the worst of the conflict, was in fact a colossal blunder, because it emboldened the Muslim leadership not to make concessions to the Cutilheiro requirements for a cantonal tripartite internal division of the country but to endure on the road to what they called the republic of citizens, Gradjanska Drzava which was de facto the concept of a more or less centralised, more or less unitary Bosnia. By insisting on that concept, they fell into the same trap that the Serbian leadership of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia fell between the two world wars. That is, trying to impose administrative unity from above in the face of ethnic diversity from below. For King Alexander to embark on that experiment in 1929 was an act of folly. For Izetbegovic to persist with the same demand in 1992 simply defies belief.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Dr. Trifkovic, can you now specifically explain to us your opinion as an academic historian again and political scientist again, the effect of the developments in the B and H, the Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Those who have read my report will immediately understand that my overall attempt was to contextualise the events in Prijedor and place them in the broader context of the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole n Croatia, in Belgrade, in Brussels, in Washington DC and elsewhere. It is no more possible to write an isolated history of the Prijedor municipality in the Bosnian wars of 1992 to 1995, than it is possible to write the history of the city of Toledo in the Spanish Civil War of 1936 to 1939 in isolation from what was going on in the rest of Spain or the history of the city of Richmond in Virginia, in the war between the States of 1861 to 1865 in isolation from what was going on on the battlefields and in Washington and in Atlanta and elsewhere around the United States. The city of Prijedor was in a way a microcosm of Bosnian divisions, Bosnian fears, Bosnian expectations, Bosnian hopes, and as I have tried to indicate, both the actions of the SDA in the municipality, notably the refusal to appoint number 2 in the local Ministry of the Interior, i.e., the commander of the police station, and the Serbian response, which often was an improvised and ad hoc affair, both seemed to have been imported from without. Furthermore, the tensions in the municipality towards the end of 1991 were greatly heightened by the events next door in Croatia, by the influx of Serb refugees from Croatia, who also brought the tales of terror that sounded eerily reminiscent of the events still very much in the living memory of many Prijedorians from the period of 1941 to 1945. And the mobilisation of the reservists, their stint on the Slavonian front and their return home, all of which created the sense that events were spiralling out of control and that no matter what the decisions on the ground, cosmic forces were at play, that events were getting out of their own hands and that they will be just the chess pieces in a much bigger game than that concerning the Prijedor municipality. This doomsday feeling also prompted many citizens of Prijedor to pack up and leave well before the first shots were fired, with the somewhat predictable pattern of departures of Muslims and Croats to Croatia and on to Austria and Germany where many of them had their family members as guests workers, gastarbeiters and many Serbs heading east to Belgrade, Novi Sad and other places in Serbia. Also, in the run-up to the beginning of the war itself, I think it is important to emphasise, and this is something that I did not include in my report, because I did not have the primary materials at my disposal then, that the functioning of the Municipal Assembly was grinding to a halt, that the financial assistance to the Prijedor municipality by the central ministries in Sarajevo was absent, that in fact from late summer of 1991, the contributions paid by the Prijedor municipality through various forms of sales tax, customs and excise, and company income, were not being recycled back, which by the beginning of 1992, created a crisis in the functioning of the key services in the municipality, such as health, social services, pensions, education and veteran affairs, that because of the lack of reproductive materials, several companies were winding down their production, and that -- and this is an opinion reflected by both Serbs and Muslims in the pages of the local newspaper, that they were being let down by Sarajevo, that they were being treated with neglect and left to stew in their own juice. I do not know to what extent this particular aspect, which I hadn't had the time to study properly, influenced this -- the feeling of hopelessness and foreboding, but it is certain that it could not have helped, particularly taking the context of the overall climate in the republic itself and the violence next door in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Dr. Trifkovic, can you also tell us what effect, if any, on Prijedor municipality had the interparty agreement, creation of Patriotic League and Green Berets, what the effect has -- was by the dispatch from Mr. Delimustafic on the 29th of April, 1992 and attacks on military convoys, if you can briefly explain to us?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Since this question is now entering into the realm of the military sequence of events, which of and by itself does not crucially impact the political, historical narrative, I would prefer not to go into detail on the domino effect, if you will, of actions, counteractions, causes and effects. In fact, my understanding was, when I was doing the final version of my background report, that it would more or less end with the beginning of the shooting war in the municipality of Prijedor and so short of saying that what I already said on Friday, that it always matters a great deal who fired the first shots because the beginning of violence has incalculable momentum of its own, I would rather not try to evaluate the specific impact of any one step in the subsequent equation because I expect the military expert will deal with that in some detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor. May I ask you, then, do you have an opinion, based upon a reasonable degree of certainty, as an academic historian and political scientist, whether the takeover in the Prijedor municipality was part of a joint criminal enterprise to ethnically cleanse B and H?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please rephrase your question because you are mixing judicial terms with terms normally used by historians and political experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Doctor, I have to rephrase my question and I'll ask you, can you tell us what effect did the takeover have on various ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: What we were witnessing in Bosnia and Herzegovina in April and May of 1992, is the process of establishment of territorial control by the political organs of different ethnic groups, almost invariably corresponding to the numeric preponderance of a given ethnic group in a given locality. An unsurprising corollary of such takeovers was the sense of insecurity of the minority ethnic group or the ethnic group which was not in power in a given locality, so that, quite unsurprisingly, I emphasise, Serbs and Muslims would not regard the HVO control over the city of Mostar as something to be welcomed or regarded with indifference. Likewise, the Serbs left in the centre of Sarajevo did not feel that they had a stake in the resulting order. And so I think it is not surprising that the Muslims in the Prijedor municipality did not regard the SDS takeover as something that they would either welcome or readily identify with, but at the same time, if you look at the period between the takeover itself and the violent escalation in the municipality with the shoot-outs at Hambarine and then in the city of Prijedor itself, at the very end of May, you do not get the impression that anything particularly drastic or dramatic was taking place. In fact, from the published sources, one gets the impression that events start veering towards a violent reckoning only after the shooting war started in the municipality. Also, I believe that it was Dr. Stakic's explicit desire, judging by the published sources, to allay the fears of the non-Serbs and to explain the establishment of the Serb control over the municipality strictly in terms of the need to enable the functioning of the municipal organs and to have a continuous provision of services. Whereas I find it hard to judge to what extent Dr. Stakic's statements reflected consensual view of the SDS leadership in Prijedor as a whole, I think it is remarkable that if and when a conciliatory tone were required, it seems that almost invariably it was he who was used as the conduit for such statements, either because he had already enjoyed a reputation of a person with conciliatory frame of mind or because such reputation had been established through his statements in the run-up to the dramatic events we are dealing with today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There are many more issues that we would like to discuss with you, doctor, some of which are address in your report, however, the time constraints imposed at this time, we have no more questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know whether Your Honour has imposed time constraints but if Mr. Lukic feels there are other matters to be covered with the doctor, then I think he ought to be enabled to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You were first on your feet. Than I had the possibility to answer. I am not aware of any time constraints imposed on you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Dr. Trifkovic has some other commitments and we discussed it previously the last week, so we set --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I read carefully the transcript of last week. Maybe for this purpose in open court, ask you when is it absolutely necessary that you have to leave this friendly country of the Netherlands?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Netherlands is very much a friendly country to me. Two of my daughters are half Dutch and one of them still lives in this country so I feel almost at home here. The problem is not so much being here but having my fairly busy scheduled totally thrown off balance so the answer is I absolutely should have been back in Chicago yesterday, but that being neither here nor there if there is any possibility of wrapping up my testimony in the course of today, I would be greatly appreciative. Of course, I realise it's up to the Court to decide whether this is indeed possible or not, but I am more or less reconciled to all kinds of problems that I will have to deal with as the result of my staying on this week, and in that spirit, I throw myself at your mercy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think your testimony is of that importance that there in fact should be no kind of limitation of the Defence, and therefore, I invite you, if possible, to continue with your extremely interesting analysis, if necessary until tomorrow, but this would be then the absolute deadline. Would this be feasible for you, also in light that you have scheduled your lectures for Thursday and Friday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were already cancelled now because I wasn't sure what was going to happen so I couldn't keep them in abeyance. Since I have the microphone right now, on Friday I was asked by Mr. Lukic to elaborate on the issue of the impact of the mujahedin from around the world making their appearance in Bosnia and using Bosnia as a staging base for their operations elsewhere around the world. Again, since I didn't expect that question, I wasn't able to provide a detailed and documented answer but thanks to the wonders of Federal Express, I now have four copies of my latest book, "The Sword of the Profit. Islam: History, Theology, Impact on the World." And in the chapter 5, page 217, there is a subchapter dealing with this very issue. So I have these four copies. Maybe one for OTP, one for Defence and two for the Bench in case you deem it useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this. May I ask the usher to distribute it? It would be then for the Defence to tender, if necessary, these documents. So this would be provisionally marked D94 but maybe, based on questions by the Defence, you can elaborate a little bit more on this, what you're discussing in your book, but may I ask the Defence, in the light of what we have just heard, to continue with the line of their questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Trifkovic, can you tell us now what was the impact of early appearance in mujahedins in Bosnia and Herzegovina and whatever you deem necessary to explain this issue?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Already in the period before the beginning of Yugoslavia's disintegration, in the 1970s and the 1980s, while Yugoslavia was a prominent member of the so-called non-aligned movement, a sort of special relationship was being developed between Bosnia-Herzegovina and certain non-aligned countries in the Arab world, and Tito's policy of close friendship with the Arabs and most notably his special relationship with the late Egyptian leader, Gamal Abdel Nasser, led to the provision of special educational facilities for hundreds of Bosnian students in such establishments as the main Islamic university in Cairo, and various other institutions of higher learning in the Muslim world, in places such as Tripoli in Libya, Kuwait and Damascus. The result of this was also the financial assistance from the Arab world for the construction of mosques in Bosnia-Herzegovina so that during this non-aligned period in the late 1970s and in the aftermath of Tito's death in the 1980s, the number of new religious objects built in Bosnia-Herzegovina exceeded that built during the entire Ottoman period between the 1460s and the 1870s. So with the outbreak of the war, or rather with the on set of the crisis that led to the outbreak of the war, strong and enduring links had already been developed between the Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina and various segments in the Arab and Islamic world, not least Alasna [phoen] University, Saudi Arabia, Libya, and a prominent example of this connection was Haris Silajdzic who was, for instance, instrumental in arranging the visit by Alija Izetbegovic to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia why at the end of March, 1992, at a very delicate moment, when the Cutilheiro plan seemed in imminent danger of collapse and international recognition of Bosnia was looming large. Nevertheless, the arrival of the so-called mujahedin from different parts of the Islamic world to Bosnia was not regarded as a welcome development even by many Muslims, who were taken aback by -- I'm talking about Bosnian Muslims, of course -- who were taken aback by the single-minded fanaticism, by the blood lust and by the lack of even rudimentary balanced view of the place they were in and the objectives they were fighting on the part of the newly arrived volunteers, who by the way started terrorising local Muslim population in the areas where they established themselves, notably in a village near Travnik, forcing women to cover their heads, forcing men to grow beards, and generally behaving the way that I suppose the Jihadists would behave everywhere trying to impose their code of conduct and their view of the world on those under their sway. Also their method of warfare itself and, in particular, their savage treatment of prisoners with well-documented cases of decapitation of Serb prisoners, such video tapes were even sold in Islamic centres around the western world until not so long ago, even for the denizens of the Balkans who were brutalised by mutual experiences, this was something qualitatively new, the notion of saving prisoners if for no other reason than to exchange them for one's own on the other side was alien to these mujahedin. Additional problem was created for the rest of the world by the fact that many of them were given Bosnian citizenship and issued Bosnian passports and were thus able to move across European borders with less difficulty than would have been the case had they retained Pakistani or Saudi or Algerian, or some other nationality of the countries that provide the bulk of terrorist suspects these days. In the book I provide a fairly detailed list of documented cases of terrorism, Islamic terrorism, springing out of Bosnia, ending with the spring of 2002, which was the time when the manuscript went to the printers. Beyond that date, the portfolio has grown and I'm sure that people better acquainted with the work of western intelligence services would be more qualified than I am to give you the precise road map, but suffice to say that at least following the departure of Alija Izetbegovic from the position of Bosnian president, we have witnessed an attempt by the authorities in Sarajevo to put an end to the misuse and abuse of Bosnian hospitality by the mujahedin and that in particular, in the aftermath of September 11th, the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina have made a serious effort to confront this menace, well aware that the failure to do so would expose them to all kinds of suspicions and accusations which are not in their own interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you an extremely trivial question? On the top line of your book, one can read, the political incorrect guide to Islam. Is this headline one by the editors, in order to better sell this book? Or is it on purpose from your own political view to provide, to a certain extent, a provocative other view on the Islam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since you put me on the spot like this I'll have to answer frankly, it's a marketing stunt by the publishers. I was personally opposed to it because I felt that it lowered the tone, if you will, but in their wisdom, they opted for this little addendum, and it seems to have worked because the book is now within the five best selling titles dealing with Islam in the United States, so who am I to complain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just to be sure that it's not an expression of your own view but it would be the incorrect guide? Okay. Mr. Lukic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that I finalised this issue if Dr. Trifkovic doesn't have anything else to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But you mentioned beforehand that you would have number of additional questions and in the light of the limited time, you said you didn't want to put forward these questions but please do so. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. But also we said that everything is in the Dr. Trifkovic's report so we don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then it would be for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Madam Korner, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Dr. Trifkovic, when were you first instructed to prepare this report?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: At first I was not instructed to prepare it. I was approached by Mr. Ostojic, who I had known personally for some years, with a view to my potential role as an expert witness for the Defence. After a number of rather sporadic meetings at several weeks distance, being the period of September, October, I think that we've clarified the shape and the terms of the report sometime in November of last year, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what were the terms of reference that you were given?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: I explained to Dr. -- to Mr. Ostojic that I do not have much interest in the -- to use the colloquial term of the nitty-gritty of who did what to whom, when and how in the municipality of Prijedor. But having read the two reports of Professor Donia, both the shorter one dealing with Prijedor itself and the longer one dealing with Bosnian Krajina, I felt that where I could provide an useful contribution would be to place the events in Prijedor in the broader context of events in Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole and broader than that, within the context of the Yugoslav crisis and the diplomatic moves connected with it. And I -- in some ways, my -- the eventual shape of my report is the result of my suggestion to Mr. Ostojic as to where I felt I could provide a useful input rather than his specific instructions to me as to what the report ought be like. In other words, it was, one might say, a two-way process where we worked out my potential useful role in providing the historical and political background to the events in Prijedor for this Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Dr. Trifkovic, I understand that you want to leave if possible today. I think that's unlikely. I think if you can try and cut your answers down, is the simple answer to the question I asked that there were no terms of reference? In other words, you were not handed a letter setting out your terms of reference?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: I was not handed a letter setting out my terms of reference but we did reach the verbal agreement about the terms of reference towards the end of November of last year, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So your understanding from your conversations over a period of weeks with Mr. Ostojic, was that you were to write a report putting the events in Prijedor into historical perspective?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Historical and political perspective, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How long did it take you to write this report?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: I prepared the first draft of the report shortly after Christmas. In fact, in the first week of the new year. Mr. Ostojic was travelling along --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I -- how long? A hundred hours, 200 hours, 50 hours?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: I would say 120 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's the full report?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Including reading the documents that were produced by Mr. Lukic, the three binders?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: It is unfortunate that the -- that many of the subsequent documents were given to me after the report was completed. My report was completed in the second week of February of this year and it is in the aftermath of that event that further translations of articles from both Kozarski Vjesnik and Oslobodenje were made available to me. Some of those materials are very useful and had I had them at my disposal earlier than that I would certainly have made use of those materials in my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, why did you need translations? You read --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do but it is my understanding that unless a document is actually entered as a translated document into the court records, and given a reference number, that I cannot use it at face value in my report under the -- and make reference to it in foot notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want to come on to the documents you looked at in a moment. Am I right in supposing that you have no legal training at all?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: I did have a course in international law while I was studying international relations but it was more years ago than I care to remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So the answer is apart from that, you're not a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've never done any legal --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Apart from this? Thank you. In order to prepare this report, did you speak to Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I met Dr. Stakic twice here at -- in the Scheveningen jail once for half an hour, once for closer to an hour in October of last year.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why was that? Why did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Primarily because I felt that before I take on the task, I wanted to create my own impression of the man. I believe in intuition. I believe in assessing a person on the basis of firsthand contact, and I felt that this was an issue of such importance, such magnitude, and such potential weight for my personal state of mind, if you will, and as well as professional reputation, that I wouldn't feel at ease undertaking the task if I had the feeling that the person was being devious, duplicitous, that I was -- if I had problems with Dr. Stakic as a person, as the result of those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So is your opinion of Dr. Stakic, which you've given to this Court, based as much on your meeting with him over approximately one and a half hours as the documentation that you read?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not. The meetings, as I said, purely had a purpose of establishing a non-scientific sense of the person that had no impact on the contents of my report but simply had a lot to do with my decision to undertake writing it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see. And when did you see Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was one day in September and one day in the first week of October. On both occasions, I was in Europe on a different business, and I made detours to The Hague for the purpose of those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The Court was told in a document that related to your proposed evidence, that you were going to provide the Honourable Court with an objective overview of the history in the region of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In your view, is your report and what you've told us an objective view?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: The issue of objectivity in the social sciences and human affairs is as old as those sciences themselves and without dwelling on the philosophical issues involved, I would say yes, that it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you have been described quite a lot as a historian and an academic historian, and a political scientist. Am I right in assuming that as a historian, you would regard yourself as a responsible historian?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As a journalist, which you told us was another aspect of your working career, would you regard yourself as a responsible journalist?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: I'm less proud of my journalistic career than I am of my academic career. Unlike many journalists who have an exalted view of their profession, I do not think that journalists are, by and large, particularly responsible lot, but certainly when it comes to the coverage of affairs Yugoslav or affairs ex-Yugoslav, I think I have been more responsible than most.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And by that, can I give an example? You wouldn't rush into print without checking the accuracy of the information that you were going to give in an article?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Rushing into print and checking accuracy are very often extremely contradictory demands, as all too many journalists covering former Yugoslav affairs have had opportunity to find out. Let me simply say that I would never knowingly rush into print with a piece of information I was aware of as being erroneous.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Or make serious allegations of impropriety or illegality or something of that nature without at least attempting to ensure that the basis for these allegations was there?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Not without at least attempting to ascertain otherwise, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the same, I take it, even more so as a historian, you would want to check very carefully your facts before you went into print on a particular aspect of history?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: As a historian, I can only say that my articles are almost invariably subject to peer review, and that therefore even if there was the problem of rushing into print, as you put it, it would be picked up and corrected by the process of refereeing articles to which my scholarly articles in the quarterlies and in the books are invariably subjected.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The basic documents for a historian to look at, first of all, are those that were created at the time. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: There are three groups of documents. One would be the formal documents of the political, military and diplomatic bodies and personalities involved. One would be firsthand memoirs, accounts, testimonies, interviews. And the third would be impartial observer accounts, reminiscences. So it would be what you mention is one of the three groups of documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: One of the difficulties, isn't it, with memoirs and the like is that they are filtered, as it were, through the selective memory of the person who is publishing them.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: That is quite so but at the same time, we shouldn't give undue credence to documents themselves either because very often, even as they are being created, they are being written with a view to self-justifying narrative of the events in the time to follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But they are better in each case, are they not, than second-hand accounts from other books; for example, other historians who have written about these events?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes and no. In one particular area, in the -- that is, for instance, the constitutional imbroglio involving Bosnia-Herzegovina, I found other authors more lucid and more clearly -- better capable of defining the problems and offering their own view of the solutions than the documents themselves, because no matter how many times you read the decisions of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the Serbs taking exception to those decisions and criticising them, when you look at, for instance, Robert Hayden's book on the constitutional aspects of the Bosnian crisis, the issues are spelt out with a degree of clarity and coherence that primary sources are never capable of telling of and by themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to deal in a moment with the various books that you've referred to in your report. Mr. Hayden, whom you've just mentioned, do you know him personally?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: I met him last in 1994 at AAASS convention in Pittsburg. I have met him, I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you aware that he had testified at this Tribunal as well?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He didn't tell you that he'd testified in the Tadic case?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: I met him in 1994. I suspect it was before his testimony in the Tadic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In this particular case, from what I understand you to say, this is the first time you've been asked to look at Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And before that, other than the name, did you have any knowledge about the events in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: I was certainly aware of Prijedor being mentioned in connection with the events of the summer of 1992. I also followed with some interest the controversy surrounding the so-called "picture that shook the world" with Penny Marshall, ITN, and Deichman's article.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You looked at, if we look at your report and the documents that were supplied, a number of newspaper articles, a great many newspaper articles; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. In the aftermath of my visit here in October of last year, I took with me a number of copies of Kozarski Vjesnik from the period under review and I incorporated most of those articles relevant to the period.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And do I also understand, looking at the list of documents, that you read books written by the Muslim side of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: In addition, I would mention, because I'm not sure any more which ones I referred to in the report and which ones I read subsequently, but there is a whole array of articles by Muslim authors on the period of the founding of the Patriotic League. While I was doing the report I know I had used Halilovic's book, "Cunning Strategy," but there is also a whole host of serialised articles on the early days of the League and the beginnings of the Green Berets in different locations all over Bosnia published by the Dani magazine as well as by the Oslobodenje daily.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You also refer in your report to a number of other authors. For example, Noel Malcolm whom you criticise somewhat.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Only in passing. I did read his short history of Bosnia but I did not find it particularly useful for the purposes of my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And you told the Court last week - and this is page 59 of the LiveNote for the 13th of March - that: "In view of my extensive experience, personal as well as professional interest in the wars of Yugoslav succession, the primary source was, of course, my accumulated and varied collection of experiences, both concerning personal contacts and primary and secondary sources." And you stand by that, do you?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you look at any of the SDS minutes for the Prijedor municipality for this period?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: I did look at the December document. I believe it's December 19th, 1991, known as variant A and variant B. I did not see any specific minutes of SDS meetings other than that particular one. I did, however, see a number of articles in Kozarski Vjesnik relating, relevant to the various SDS events, including reports of their meetings and statements by their leading personalities after those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you aware that the Defence were in possession of the book of the SDS meetings in 1991 and 2? Or 1992, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You weren't aware?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ask whether there were any original documents produced at the time which you could see?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: I did not specifically ask for SDS related documents. I did ask for any useful sources that could assist me in the preparation of my report, and in connection with that I was given the document both in original and translation called, "Variant A and B" as well as Kozarski Vjesnik articles and the subsequent folders which, unfortunately, came after my report had already been written.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I understand you to say that you've just -- that you've looked at a large number of newspaper articles and some of the memoirs. What I'm asking you about is documents relating to these events produced at the time. Did you, for example, know that there were records of the municipal assembly meetings in Prijedor available?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware that there were meetings of the municipal assembly of Prijedor available.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because you make a number of comments in your report about the events. Would it have helped you, do you think, to compile your report, to have seen these documents?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: It depends. Very often - and I've seen minutes of different meetings of different bodies in different contexts, not the one in Prijedor - such minutes only blur the issue and make it more difficult to sift the occasional grain of gold from tonnes of sand than would otherwise be the case. I would be very pleasantly surprised if any of those minutes would qualitatively throw a -- would throw a qualitative new light on the overall pattern of events as outlined in my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So in your view, as a historian, it is better -- you are more likely to get a better picture of the events from newspaper articles? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm saying that while indeed it would have been very useful to have access to primary sources, that those primary sources of and by themselves would not necessarily change the overall picture of events that I present, because let me emphasise again, in the events leading up to Yugoslavia's disintegration and from its disintegration into wars of Yugoslav succession, the primary documents concerning meetings of political bodies seem to have often had the objective of providing ex post facto justification for those bodies for what they were doing as they were doing it. So without passing judgement on the minutes of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly meetings, I'm simply trying to say that it would be a pleasant surprise for me, once I look at them, if they were capable of throwing a qualitatively new light on the fundamental assumption that I am taking in my report, which is the events in Prijedor were reactive to the broader Bosnian context and not proactive in and of themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I understand that -- we'll deal with your report after the break, but your general case is that the Serbs were reacting to effectively the positions taken by the Muslims and the Croats. But I want to -- I want to make sure I understand this. Are you saying that the -- what was being recorded in the minutes of the SDS party of the municipal assembly was all being said with an eye to the future?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that what was being said at the SDS assembly alone was being said with an eye to the future. I have stated, and I am not the first one to do so, that on all sides, there was a certain - how shall I put it? - desire to provide a manoeuvring space when it comes to the verdict of history, so that not only on the SDS side but on other sides too, decisions that had very clear political meaning in the sense of one party's interests and objectives were couched in the language that at least gave the appearance of appealing to the interests of other parties and satisfying the requirements of other parties' interests.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't want to spend too long on this, Dr. Trifkovic. Is the situation this: That you didn't inquire whether any of this type of documentation was available for you to see because you don't believe that it could have assisted you?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: No, as I said earlier, I did inquire what was available. I believe had these documents been available to me, I would have certainly gladly read them and made use of them in my report. I was not aware of their existence, but I'm simply adding, as a personal comment, that even without seeing these particular documents that you're referring to but having seen various other contemporary minutes, that we shouldn't trust too much even into the so-called primary sources because the actors in historical events, being aware of making history, very often have a way of distorting the minutes of ongoing events and couching them in the language that suits the way they want to be perceived in the future.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just finally on this, I think, because it's time for a break, have you at any stage read the records of the assembly meetings at republic level?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: I did read the minutes of the 14th of October debate, or rather, the debate preceding the vote on the 14th of October, when the memorandum on the independent and sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina was adopted by the SDA-HDZ MPs. I also followed the statements by the SDS board when they called for the plebiscite of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina on November 9th of 1991. The statement -- sorry, these were not minutes of the assembly. The actual minutes of the assembly that I did read concerned the debate in advance of the vote on the memorandum.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So, I'm sorry, does this mean to say in the whole of your career as a historian in respect of events in Bosnia, the only minutes of the assemblies that you have ever read are those of the 14th, 15th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Good Lord, no. I thought you were asking specifically when we are talking about my report here. I also read very carefully, but it was not relevant to the report, the debate of the Republika Srpska assembly concerning the acceptance of the Vance-Owen Plan in the spring of 1993. I wasn't sure about your question. I thought you were specifically asking me when it comes to the period under review, which is the period from the multi-party election until the events of May of 1992, I believe that the debate that preceded the vote on the memorandum was in many ways most significant because it spelt out the relevant positions of the three interested parties more clearly and more nakedly, if you will, than anything that had preceded it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It is -- Dr. Trifkovic, the trial stays adjourned now until 5 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Dr. Trifkovic, I want to ask you about one more set of minutes of assembly meetings. Have you ever read the minutes of the 16th session of the assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, held on the 12th of May, 1992 in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not read the minutes themselves. I have read the accounts of the session but not the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Didn't you think it was important, not only for this case but for your knowledge as a historian of the events of 1992, to read the original minutes?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Since you insist so much on the issue of the minutes of different sessions, let me make a general comment concerning the selection of sources. In the frankly unlimited deluge of different minutes, whether it's the Herceg-Bosna assembly in Mostar, whether it's the BH Muslim-dominated government in Sarajevo, or the Republika Srpska organs of different kinds, if one were to try and process the particular original documents in their entirety, we are not looking at 100 or 120 hours, which I was allotted for this task, but easily five or ten times more. I believe that very often when we look at historical events, if we get to the minutiae, to the nitty-gritty of who said what, where and when, we lose sight, let me reiterate, of the key decisions by the key decision makers. And quite frankly, both in the case of the different assemblies on both sides of the ethnic divide and lower ranking officials, the statements are of far lesser importance than the key determinants of the decision making elite, whether it's the Izetbegovic-Ganic-Silajgic triumvirate on one side or Karadzic-Krajisnik-Koljevic triumvirate on the other. So with due respect, even though I do not think that minutes are unimportant per se, I do not think that going through the detailed minutes of different assemblies on different sides of the divide would fundamentally or materially alter the overall picture that I tried to provide in my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, are you saying that the statements of the leaders on both sides about what their goals and objectives were during 1992, are not important?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: No, on the contrary, what I'm saying is that what those leaders have stated on different occasions, and in particular I'm referring to the Assembly in Banja Luka that you mentioned, the strategic objectives of the Serbian side, even in the second rendering, are more important than reading the -- every word of the minutes per se. In other words, I do not think that it is particularly important to read the original document in order to acquire the overall picture of what was the political drift, what was the, if you will, broad picture, rather than what was the specific statement of which party at which step of the way. So if we were to say that on the 12th of May, the Serb leadership has stated the strategic objectives of the conflict, as far as they were concerned, I think that even with the second re-summary contained in various sources that I have had access to, I can form as good a picture as to what was going on in Banja Luka as if I had actually read the minutes themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you are aware that that is where the Serbs set out their six strategic goals?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that that is where the enumeration of the six so-called strategic goals was stated, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why so-called?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Because I do not think that in an objective sense, the six have quite the same strategic significance. In other words, the fact that they themselves chose to call them strategic doesn't make them equally strategic. I think that on the Serb side there had always been a tendency to confuse quantitative aspects, such as maps, territorial delineations, with what I believe were far more important and substantive constitutional issues, so much so that Karadzic's propensity to draw maps was something of a standing joke even on the Serbian side, from the very early days. So in reply to your question, they may have called their six objectives strategic. I think that as far as the Serbs were concerned, there should have been only one real strategic objective and that is to have themselves recognised as one of the constituent nations of Bosnia-Herzegovina without whose agreement no change in its constitutional status could be legally effected.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you accept that one of those goals, separation from those who are our enemies, and who have used every opportunity, especially in this century to attack us and who would continue with such practices if we were to continue to stay together in the same state, and I am quoting from page 00913513 of Exhibit S141, was in effect a statement of ethnic separation?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that statement was a carbon copy of a statement issued by the gathering of Muslim intellectuals at Dom Milicija, the militia hall in Sarajevo on 10th of June of 1991, where they stated that with the separation of Croatia and Slovenia from Yugoslavia, which by the way had not taken place on that date, it was yet to happen within a fortnight, that they would not stay within Yugoslavia because they would not risk being subjected to genocide and disappearance. In other words, the statement of the Serb Assembly on 12th of May of 1992 reflected the same sentiment that was present in the Muslim elite's statement from almost a year previously, 11 months previously, and that is the reluctance of one ethnic group to remain in a polity in which it would be dominated by the members of another ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you refer to that document when you were preparing your report? The Muslim document that you've just talked about.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: I may have referred to the Muslim decision to go ahead with separation in case of Croatia's and Slovenia's secession without specifically referring to that document. I cannot immediately recall whether I quote the document or not. But I'm that sure you have the record of that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you have that document here?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe instead of the document itself, I have the reference to the -- that gathering being made by various Muslim memoirists, including Sefer Halilovic, including Sulejman Vran and others. In other words, if you ask me what I have here is reference to that gathering in Dom Milicija by a variety of Muslim sources.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you -- is the answer to the question no, you don't have the document?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the document itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen the document itself?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: What I have seen is the accounts of the gathering, because the gathering itself was confidential and I do not know if the formal record of the gathering exists.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So the answer to the question, Dr. Trifkovic, is you have never seen a document setting out the assertion you've just made?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen a variety of Muslim sources, a variety of Muslims, who were present at that session, talking about the decisions of the gathering of the Muslim intellectuals, even there is a number of the directive which they issued and since they coincide, I have no reason to believe, and since they are not mutually contradictory, I have no reason to believe that they do not correspond to the facts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I would like just to put one more speech from this Assembly to you, Dr. Trifkovic, a speech made by Dr. -- I'm sorry, a man named Dragan Kalinic. This is at page 00913522. Who stated in the middle -- at the beginning of his speech, rather, "Among all the issues, this Assembly should decide on, the most important one is this: Have we chosen the option of war or the option of negotiation? I say this with a reason, and I must instantly add that knowing who our enemies are, how perfidious they are, how they cannot be trusted, until they are physically, militarily destroyed and crushed, which of course implies eliminating and liquidating their key people." Have you ever read that speech before, Dr. Trifkovic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen reference to it. I have not read the speech in the original. I admit this is very strong language of the kind that we unfortunately encountered on all sides at this moment in Bosnian imbroglio and that when it comes to war speech, and this is undoubtedly what may be classed as war speech, it started in the context of Bosnia-Herzegovina with a remarkable statement by Alija Izetbegovic from over a year earlier that for the sake of peace, he would not sacrifice Bosnia's sovereignty, and he -- sorry, that he would not choose peace over sovereignty and he would not sacrifice sovereignty for the sake of peace.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you quote that in your report and I'll come to that later. So your view objective as you are, is that this speech and what was said in the 12th of May Assembly generally, is a reaction to what was said by the Muslim side in 1991?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Not only in 1991. I was again, if we are seeking a modicum of objectivity, which is always difficult when we encounter events which we know to have resulted in tragic outcomes, there was a clear sequence of proactive events on the Muslim side creating reaction on the Serbian side. The seminal event, as I tried to indicate in my examination-in-chief last Thursday and Friday evening, was the illegal vote by Muslim and Croat MPs in the Bosnian assembly on October 14th --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't want to stop you, Doctor, but I'm going to come to that. I'm going to come to that in your report.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: So various moves on the part of the proactive side created responses on the reactive side. I think it stands to reason that the Serbs had a reactive posture because, after all, they were the ones who wanted to preserve the status quo of Bosnia as part of Yugoslavia, and it's also unremarkable and unsurprising that the Muslim-Croat tactical alliance was proactive because it wanted to change that status, and to change it even, if need be, in disregard of Bosnia's own constitution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told us that you saw the document which is generally known as variant A and B.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ask to see it or were you given it?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: I was given it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you also given the minutes of the meeting of the Serbian democratic party in Prijedor on the 27th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you aware that there were such minutes where this document was discussed?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would that have been something that you would have thought was useful in your discussion of the events of Prijedor as they related to the larger events?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Quite possibly so, but without seeing them, I'm not able to comment with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to for a moment ask you a couple of questions about your career. You told us that you were an adviser, this was in your original examination-in-chief on the 13th of March, that -- forgive me -- you were a political consultant to, amongst others, Crown Prince Alexander of Yugoslavia, the Republika Srpska, and the now former president of Yugoslavia, Dr. Kostunica, plus a variety of private companies. Were you also an adviser to Biljana Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: In the period of February to July of 1998, I was the adviser to president -- then president of Republika Srpska, Biljana Plavsic, for relations with the Serbian diaspora, in which capacity I organised her visit to the United States and Canada in May of that year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt but we have not come back to this. In your own annex 1, you pointed out that you had been an adviser to the Dr. Biljana Plavsic as from 1997 already.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In late 1997 I corresponded with letter in an informal capacity, providing my views on the way in which the Dayton framework was being perceived in the Western world and different attitudes to the pursuance of that framework on both sides of the Atlantic, but it was only in the period February, or rather, March of 1998 to July of 1998, that this relationship had a formalised character. In other words, it was a part-time consultancy engagement for me at a small monthly retainer, but in the period of November 1997 to March 1997 [sic] it had an informal and non-remunerary character.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do we take it that you got to know Mrs. Plavsic reasonably well during this period?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: During this period, I not only got to know Mrs. Plavsic reasonably well but I accepted the assignment on the understanding that she was wholly committed to the Dayton process and was frankly regarded as persona grata [Realtime transcript read in error "gratan"] in the Western power centres [Realtime transcript read in error "person power centres"]. As someone who had, unlike many other people interested in things Serbian, someone who had regarded, always regarded the Dayton framework as the best deal the Serbs could hope for under the circumstances, I believed that she should be helped in clarifying the position of the Republika Srpska in terms of standing behind Dayton 100 per cent but behind the letter of Dayton and not some nebulous spirit of Dayton that had the hidden agenda of salami slicing Republika Srpska into oblivion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, just that the transcript is clear on page 42, line 12, one can't read -- it reads here, she was frankly regarded as "gratan." Persona grata, you said, or persona non-grata.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Persona grata.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Persona grata. Okay, thank you. And then you continued "in Western power centres," not "in person power centres," correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you also the spokesman and chief of the Republika Srpska bureau in London?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: In the period between November of 1993 and July of 1994, an attempt was made by me to institute an unofficial representative office of the Republika Srpska in London. When I say "attempt," after all these years, all I can say in full frankness to the Court is that the failure to turn it into an ongoing concern was the total lack of informational coherence on the Serbian side, the impossibility of establishing clear channels of communication, and of regular two-way inputs which would at least enable me, as very often the person asked to give interviews and take part in university debates, round tables and the like, and which had resulted in my personal decision to terminate that relationship in August of 1994, and from that point on, in all of my public utterances and media contacts, I acted as the Balkan affairs analyst with close links to the Bosnian Serbs, which enabled me to speak with greater authority; in other words, not to be held accountable for, frankly, what was a blunderous and often incoherent position emanating from Pale. This, to some extent, was also due to the fact that on the Republika Srpska side, the system of external communication was made extremely difficult by the appointment of Dr. Karadzic's daughter as the head of the international press centre and made my own attempts to communicate with Pale in order to give some credence to the putative existence of the representative office in London well nigh impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Dr. Trifkovic, is there any reason why that doesn't appear on your CV?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: What doesn't appear?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That you were the representative of the Republika Srpska between November, 1993 and July, 1994, in London.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, my consulting engagements for Republika Srpska cover -- in other words, I didn't elaborate on the types of duties that I had with HRH Crown Prince Aleksandar's office in 1992-93; I didn't elaborate on the kind of duties I performed for Biljana Plavsic in 1998; I didn't elaborate on the kind of information input that I was providing to President Kostunica in 2000 and 2001. So the only reason is that, first of all, the status of my putative representation was both legally and substantively moot; and secondly, because even in terms of my own relationship with Pale, it remained somewhat murky, and in the end, ended in what I have to admit was the failure to establish the reasonable level of coherence and two-way communication that would give real substance to something that didn't move beyond the name and the title.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So it would be wrong, would it, to suggest to you that the reason it's omitted is because it might reduce your appearance as an objective historian of this period?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, absolutely. And at no time did I intend to either conceal or mislead anyone regarding the existence of these connections. They are a matter of public record, including dozens of media interviews and articles dating from that period. But looking back at them, including the transcripts of my BBC and BBC World service interviews, I absolutely have nothing to regret when it comes to what I hope was a reasonably accurate and informative presentation of what I can only now call generic Serb point of view rather than specifically Republika Srpska point of view, because as I say, due to the lack of developed system of bureaucratic decision-making on the Republika Srpska side, I was in the end reduced to improvising what I could only describe as self-generated positions and scenarios which necessitated my divorcing myself from any institutionalised body, even putative as it was.
