utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, Dr. Trifkovic, I have to remind you that the shorter your answers the more likely you are to be able to leave here --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: But this is of course a very delicate question and it was specifically angled at my presumed desire to conceal any element of my biography from the Court, I felt it was necessary to give a more detailed answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But it's entirely your choice, Doctor. I'm not going to stop you; I'm just reminding you. Dr. Trifkovic, what exactly is the Serbian National Defence Council of America?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Serbian National Defence Council of America came into being in 1914, in the summer of 1914, as a Serbian-American organisation founded by the famous Serbian-American scientist, Mihajlo Pupin, a close personal friend of President Woodrow Wilson, and it came into being as at that time the main conduit of humanitarian assistance and, later on, volunteers for Serbia in World War I. Its work between the two world wars was in abeyance and then it was reactivated in 1941 during World War II. In the aftermath of the war, it acted as both social and humanitarian as well as strongly anti-communist political body, recognised by the U.S. government as one of the leading Serbian-American organisations, so much so that its president is regularly invited to the "white house" for briefings given to members of ethnic groups and to social events as well as political manifestations such as the inaugural breakfast after the new administration came into power. It is an organization of the Serbian diaspora as patriotically American as simultaneously interested in things Serbian, as for instance, the Jewish American congress or the variety of Irish-American, Greek-American, Armenian-American or indeed Chinese- or Korean- or Vietnamese-American lobby groups. All of them have a great deal of interest in the developments of their old country and all of them at the same time look at those developments through the prism primarily of the interest of the ethnic diaspora in the United States and not of the old country itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And are you on the editorial board of its magazine? I think it's probably the right word, Liberty?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Liberty is the fortnightly newspaper. I am on its editorial board and I have been contributing to it with some regularity for the past five years. It was originally started during World War I. It renewed publishing during World War II. In recent years and certainly since I've been writing for it, it's been distinguished by its stringent opposition to the Milosevic regime as well as of course the view of the wars of the Yugoslav succession that take into account what I would term the generic Serb point of view rather than that which identifies itself with any particular group or personality in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So you wouldn't say that any of the positions that I've now dealt with in any way reduce your objectivity when looking at the events of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: I would in fact greatly resent your making any such suggestion, just as Morton Abramowitz would resent the suggestion that his ability to speak on Middle Eastern issues would be impaired by his membership of the Jewish-American Congress or such as Senator Edward Kennedy would resent any suggestion that his membership of Irish-American organisations impairs his ability to speak on the issues of Northern Ireland.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would you agree, Dr. Trifkovic, that you hold a deep-felt dislike, not to say hatred, of the Muslim race?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, there is no Muslim race, and the Koran is quite clear on the issue that quite the contrary, Islam is the brotherhood of the believers regardless of race and ethnicity, and the answer to your question is no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. You have on a number of occasions, I think, written articles about Islam, have you not?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: I have indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I would like to you have a look at some of them, please. I'm going to ask you be handed and the Court and the Defence, a collection of articles --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: I have seven copies of the same article.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes, sorry, they should be handed out -- I tell you what, if the usher will sort them into bundles, if the usher hands them back, we'll sort them into bundles.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, in future we will hand them out individually but I just thought it was easier to do the collection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I've put them in date order. The first, Dr. Trifkovic, dated August the 29th, 2000, "Islamic Resurgence in Nigeria; Clinton's Telling Silence." Remember that article?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You deal in some detail, with what you allege is the brutal oppression, this is in paragraph 2, of the millions of Christians inhabiting the north of the country by their Islamic rulers.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: M'hm, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I'd like you to go, please, to the second page, the third or the second full paragraph on that page. The forth line down, "Theological analysis and ethical reflection have practically disappeared from Muslim intellectual domain everywhere and in black Africa they have never developed. Contemporary Islam has thus been described as a flight from ethical concern with explicitly political objectives" and then there is a further quote from whom we don't know from this article, "Islam is thus reduced from a faith to a simplifying doctrine that justifies converting all non-believers, condemning them if they refuse, subjugating them and if they persist in refusing to submit, killing them." Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 13762 to 13773. That's a general statement. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: It is a general statement, and it partly relies on, as I put in parentheses, quotes that are not specifically mine, but yes, it is a statement that is shared most notably by Bernard Lewis and his recently published book, "What Went Wrong?" I believe that a flight from ethical concern is specifically Bernard Lewis's quote.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not interested in Mr. Lewis, whoever he may be's book. I'm interested in knowing is this your belief?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: It is my belief that in the 11th century, of the Christian era or the 5th century of the Hijira there was something that might be called the closing of the Islamic mind, after the brief flowering of the golden age of Islam in Cordoba in the west and Bagdad in the east. There was an explicit decision by the kulejma [phoen] to put an end to theological speculation which would be of an open-ended cosmological kind and to focus on the elaboration of the given body of Sunna that has been codified by that time. From that point on, for the past 900 years, what we witness in Islam is an elaboration of the legal practices and behavioural precepts that are not based upon the spirit of critical inquiry but strictly upon the theologistic regurgitation of the existing body of the primary scripture, the Koran, the Hadis [phoen], the traditions of the prophet and the Sharia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll ask you once more: Do you believe, Dr. Trifkovic, that the Islamic or Islam condemns non-believers, if they refuse to subjugation and if they persist in refusing to submit, to kill them?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: There are Koranic quotes that clearly authorise --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you, Dr. Trifkovic. I'm not interested in Koranic quotes. Is that what you believe?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: What I believe, excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you believe, this is the third time, do you believe that Islam, if they cannot subjugate non-believers, will kill them?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: There is a major body of thought in Islam that authorises killing of non-believers who refuse to submit to the faith. What Islam is, I cannot reply now. What I can say is that there are Islamic strains of thought and Islamic forms of practice. Islamic practice in Nigeria today does authorise the killing of non-believers, as we've seen with the controversy surrounding Miss World pageant that had to be cancelled a few months ago. It is unfortunate that my article was published before that time because it would provide further evidence of the problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the last time, Dr. Trifkovic S that what you believe?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we look at the next article, please? February the 27th, 2002, "Islamic Terrorism in Italy. Shape of Things to Come." If you look, please, at the second page of that article, the fourth paragraph on that page begins, "The unpleasant truth emerging from the Italian trial --" you refer to a trial that was going on -- "is that the mosques throughout the western world are being used to teach hate." Is that all mosques?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: It is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Or some?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: It is many mosques. And it -- I can elaborate on why it is so, because most mosques in the western world that were built over the past decades were financed by the Saudis, whose Wahabi strain of Islam is only vaguely comparable to the kind of stern puritanism in the Christian context and yet it is the one that is most amply endowed with petrol dollars and the one that has created, for instance, the Finsbury -- famous, notorious, Finsbury Park Mosque in north London and its many equivalents from Leicester, Birmingham and Leeds to Dearborn, Michigan, Berlin, Marseilles and Milan.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You go on to talk about Britain in this article if we look at to the bottom of the page, "Britain leads the way." If you go to the next page, page 3, second paragraph, second sentence, "In Britain today, where Islam controls the inner cities, we have major social exclusion and the development of sharia. We have had churches burned, Christians attacked, and a mission centre destroyed. The media has deliberately kept everything off the air." Which cities do you say are controlled by Islam?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: This quote is not mine. It is from the daily newspaper, the Washington Times, and it quotes an Anglican cleric, a Pakistani-born convert to Christianity, that was -- who was quoted in the article warning of what was going on in Britain but again, since you ask me I will give you some very specific answers. For instance, in the city of Oldham, the old symbol of the city, the owl, had been removed from the lampposts and signposts because the city council in which a heavy Muslim presence was established due to the demographic shift concluded that the old owl of Oldham was somehow insulting to Islamic sensibilities against graven idols and imagery. Also what I think the author of this quote is particularly referring to is not so much control of the inner cities themselves but control of the Muslim social and religious life in the inner cities. In fact, it is a standard complaint by the moderate clerics in Great Britain that their work is being undermined by the radical ones who seem to be more richly endowed with money and who have greater sway with the young -- with the young congregation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You're saying, are you, this whole paragraph from the words, "My own feeling," is a quote?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Where are the quotation marks?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: In the printout, they do not appear, because they -- the whole thing -- I don't know what programme was used, but you will see that the line above the quote doesn't -- I indicate that this is the beginning of the quote in itself in western societies, if it was my own narrative there would have been no need for the separation. And secondly, there is also the reference, reference number 1, which again relates to the entire paragraph and it is from the Washington Times of January 16th, 2002. I remember the quote well. It is, I repeat, not mine. It is from the newspaper, the Washington Times.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to the next page where you go to Germany. Meanwhile across the channel. "In Germany," you start, "the highest court in the land ruled in January 2002 that Muslim butchers should be allowed to slaughter animals according to Islamic practice, by slitting their throats and letting them bleed to death without stunning them first in any way." Do I take it that you disapprove of this decision?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: I disapprove of any decision that undermines the secular democratic tradition of western jurisprudence and constitutional tradition in favour of making exceptions that pander to the creation of special status for Islamic communities in the western world, that is but the first step to further demands which will not stop short of creating parallel sharia in addition to western jurisprudence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Does it mean that you don't accept the freedom of religion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I accept the freedom of religion but that freedom of religion has to be circumscribed by the requirements of the secular democratic society's host societies in which those immigrants have to make certain compromises. I would submit that Muslims who choose to live in Germany should be expected to make accommodation to the main stream society's mores and main stream society's constitutional and legal terms of reference and if they regard it as unacceptable, they are welcome not to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But you respect [Microphone not activated] you respect the decision by law makers and constitutional and higher courts in other countries coming to different conclusions as regards the freedom of religion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me emphasise, I think that any requirement for special treatment and exemptions, whether it is by the Muslims or for that matter, Jehovah's Witnesses, Scientologists, there have been cases concerning blood transfusion or organ transplants as life saving device, the Morman's matrimonial issues, are very dangerous, I believe, that the constitutional legal based upon the two centuries of western secularism is too precious to be undermined with special dispensations for one group or another because once you allow one exception, it may prove to be a thin wedge that may undermine the entire edifice in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The next paragraph, "Bosnian Muslims are the second largest immigrant group in Germany. They maintain close ties with the Turkish community. Already a decade ago, with a number of Muslim residents approaching 3 million, and the number of mosque associations exceeding 2.000, the writing was on the German wall." What writing?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: The writing that is stated in the following paragraph, which is again not mine, but an assessment by an Italian journalist by the name of Vittorio Messori published in Avenira in Rome in 1992. And that -- and that writing we can read, "The Turks in Berlin constitutes a social problem without a solution. There are entire sections of the city closed in on themselves, they support a parallel and hostile culture with no kind of symbiosis with the German culture and the Maghrebians have done the same thing in Marseilles, et cetera. The point that I'm trying to make and we can go on and on with the examples from France, from Britain, from Germany, is that when you have a large and compact Islamic diaspora in the western world, unlike other immigrant groups, and I am also speaking of the American experience here, unlike other immigrant groups that through the centuries, have come into these host societies and sought to integrate into those societies, to enrich the life of those societies with elements of their own culture and tradition and also to enrich themselves by accepting the dominant modes of social and political organisations in the host societies, that the Islamic diaspora is unlike any other, that it is qualitatively different in many ways and that this difference is manifested primarily in its tendency to create ghettoised forms of social and religious life that in the long term seeks to not only leave the community itself unaffected by the main stream but also to convert the host society by first seeking special dispensations and special privileges and then eventually escalating to parallel forms of social and legal and political institutions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We'll finish looking at this series of articles in a moment, Dr. Trifkovic. At the bottom of the page, "Avoiding the camp of saints, open-ended population explosion in every predominantly Muslim country in the world is underlying reality behind immigration trends. Fortifying the impression that tomorrow belongs to Islam. A Muslim woman has between five and six children on average compared to fewer than two for women in the developed world. What is the basis for that statistical analysis?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: The basis is UN statistical year books. The last I actually looked at in the connection with this article was 1989. If you look at the aggregates for the moderate countries and the Middle East and, of course, excluding Israel and allowing for some minor distortions as the result of the presence of Christian communities in Egypt, Lebanon and Syria, this is the result that you will -- that you will find for the Muslim world. For the European world, I think the picture is considerably grimmer, that in fact more recent data indicate that in Italy, in particular, as well as in Germany and France, we are not only below replacement level in Italy, I believe it is below 1.2, whereas 2.2 would be simple arithmetical replacement. I think what I'm saying here is not a matter of opinion, it is a matter of generally recognised empirically verifiable fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you aware that during the run-up to the conflict in 1992, one of the methods of scaring the Serb population was to expound on the Muslim birth rate as being much higher?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know who and how specifically referred to the problem of Muslim birth rates as a means of, as you put it, scaring the Serbs but I would be very surprised if note was not taken of the fact that indeed the birth rates of the Muslim population in the former Yugoslavia, and I think this refers more notably to Kosovo than to Bosnia, are exponentially greater than the birth rates for the Serbs or the Croats. When I was writing this article, I had -- I did not have the Yugoslav events on my mind in particular. In fact, since my focus was on Western Europe, I believe that the discrepancy in the birth rates is far greater between the majority Muslim societies of North Africa and the Middle East on the one hand and west European societies on the other than between the Bosnian Muslims on one side and the Bosnian Christians, Serbs and Croats, on the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Look at one last paragraph, please. It's over on the next page. Page 6. "It is nevertheless wrong to conclude that Muslims have simply replaced communists as the main threat to the west. They are but two faces of the same menace, of the closed society and the closed mind, and they have been the one real threat all along. "Ideological divisions have not given way to communitarian ones. The totalitarian nature of Islam, akin to communism and Naziism in aspects makes the threat different in degree to that faced during the war -- the Cold War but not in kind. It demands a similar response. Now, what response would that be?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: That response would specifically mean that prospective immigrants from the Muslim world into the western world would be subjected to very close interrogation as regards their religious and political beliefs. I submit that it is possible that there will be a reform of Islam from within. In fact, there is no doubt that moderate Islamic clerics do exist and that even the majority of ordinary Muslims are eminently moderate in their beliefs and in their daily practices but at the same time, I submit that for the time being, the vocal minorities that control political Islam and the vocal and motivated minorities that control the religious life of Islamic communities in the western world are pushing the other way, and therefore, just as to be very specific, in the Cold War, every applicant for a U.S. visa was asked if he was a member of a Communist Party, and was denied that visa if the answer was yes, unless he was coming on official business. People should be asked whether they subscribe to the variety of Islam as elaborated by Bihabism [phoen] and as presented through the hundreds of mosques in the western world, which try to find and in fact do find in their own terms, within their own analytical paradigm, the justification for violent overthrow of the existing social and political order in line with Koranic precepts and in line with the Sunna, the practices and traditions of the prophet and the historic practice of 14 centuries of political Islam. So the similar response refers primarily to the understanding that the militant strain of Islam should be treated as a subversive ideology rather than a religion, and that by now is also becoming a somewhat unremarkable view, even though when I first wrote it, may have had the character of a rather bold statement, in the meantime, I can quote a whole host of articles primarily in the United States that not only follow a similar strain of thought but also even quote me as the support of the given point of view.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The Washington Times that you say -- that the first part was a quote from, is that a newspaper that's run by something called the Unification Church?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: The Unification Church is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just answer that yes or no, please?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: It's not run by it. The Unification Church is a shareholder in the Washington Times company.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Very quickly, then, can we run through the last two of these articles--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt first that we don't lose the order, the first article would be provisional marked S400 I is the one from August 29. And the second one from February 27 would be provisional marked S410 I, but -- sorry, in order that we don't have to come back to this article, I think it's mandatory to come back to page 4 of these seven pages, when you discuss the decision and strongly criticise the decision of the German constitutional court, which of course is your right to criticise the constitutional court, but then you continue with a sentence, "If and when the constitutional court allows clitoridectomy for Germany's Muslim girls" continues, it will turn the host countries Britain, France, Germany, into an Islamic society by compelling it to adapt to their way of life, what brings you, what's the factual basis for bringing you to the insinuation that any German court could allow this clitoridectomy for Germany's Muslim girls? Aren't you aware of the contrary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is an obvious journalistic rhetorical turn of phrase that follows from Mr. Hasan Oezdogan's declaration that the decision that I referred to earlier is but an important step in the integration of Muslims in Germany. It was a deliberate piece of sarcasm implying that what in fact should be regarded as a major victory for the Muslim community that they obtained an exception to slaughter sheep and lambs the way they deem fit is but an important step. I'm implying that in terms of their own perception of what integration really means, the full integration will be achieved only if they are free to act any which way they deem fit. It was no reflection on the intentions or practices of Germany's or other countries' legal bodies. It was a reference to the Muslim activists's own perception of what they will regard as sufficient preconditions for full integration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you regard that article, as you have written here, knowing better, that the jurisprudence is absolutely the contrary, that this is a serious article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This article was written on the immediate heels of the ruling on January of 2002 and it was written in the context of a broader host of issues that included the terrorist cell being uncovered in Italy and the problem of increasing fundamentalism in Britain. I would be very curious to correct my assertions in the light of subsequent legal rulings and of course it is something of a disadvantage for me to discuss the details of the aftermath of the article with you of all people, as an expert in German constitutional affairs, but the quote that we are specifically discussing here is -- was written in the immediate aftermath of the decision of January 2002 and the triumphant statement by the head of Germany's Islamic Council commenting on that decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we get a clear view of your approach to religious freedom. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Very quickly, then, Dr. Trifkovic, the next article, December the 20th, 2002, you devoted to Britain in its entirety, entitled "The Islamic conquest of Britain."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: According to your research, in paragraph 2, "The long haul may well end up in Britain becoming an Islamic country by the end of the century with sharia law replacing common law and the Koran replacing the magnificent edifice of its unwritten constitution. If current demographic trends continue with native Britons aborting and birth controlling themselves to death, with Muslims already settled in Britain having third world birth rates, rampant immigration continuing unabated, the writing again is clearly on the wall." On what do you base this assertion that Britain may well become an Islamic country by the end of this century?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: On the extrapolation of the existing statistical trends if projected unaltered until the end of the country. There was an article in the Guardian, surprisingly so in the Guardian I say, because the Guardian is usually regarded as the mouthpiece of the liberal segment of the British establishment and therefore unlikely to dwell on the tricky issues of the demographic shift that dealt with the issue of which way Britain is heading in this respect. And I again say that this is not only an opinion from the conservative corner of Eurocentric nostalgia that laments the passing of the traditional European nations, even people who are eminently supportive of the open-ended immigration, and there was an article only this morning in the International Herald Tribune, point out that on present form, the existing population of native European countries such as Italy, France, Germany and Britain will be halved towards the end of the century and that immigration will necessarily fill up the missing jobs and that most of that immigration will come from the nearest part of the third world to Europe, which is the Maghreb North Africa and the Middle East.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You go --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: In the case of the U.K., of course, we also have the Indian subcontinent and it is a well-known fact that even from among the subcontinental immigrants, the Hindus and the Sihks have a much lower birth rates than the Muslims. In fact, the Hindu birth rates in the second generation approach those of the native population, whereas the Muslim birth rates even though they dropped compared to Pakistan or to Bangladesh where those immigrants had original nationally come from, nevertheless tend to stabilise at roughly 3 to 4 live births per woman which is still considerably higher than the native population. London already has a majority of either immigrants or second generation immigrants, and on present form, we will have contiguous and strong culturally and religiously strong pockets of more or less clear Muslim majority in a number of inner city areas. Some of them have already been established, for instance in the city of Leicester north of London, and the way that the leadership of the Islamic community in Britain right now is acting, does not bode very well for the opening up of their religious and social life in the direction of full integration and the give and take in the spirit of multi-cultural tolerance and of post modern, post-national, information-based technology in a secular democracy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Madam Korner, may I ask you not to continue with this line of questioning? I think the picture is absolutely clear, and I don't like to hear this expression of intolerance any longer in this courtroom. So we should come to another area and it should expressed -- be expressed that this Court never will attribute of any of the comments given by the expert to Dr. Stakic. We never heard such kind of expressions from Dr. Stakic. This should be quite clear. The trial stays now adjourned for 20 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated, and let us hear from the expert.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just one last question on these articles. Is this what you call responsible journalism, Dr. Trifkovic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: This is a loaded question. This is not only responsible. This is imminently factually-based journalism which seeks to establish a clear point, that there is a phenomenon called political Islam and that political Islam is a threat to western democracy as we know it. That is my considered view point and I stick by it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want to look at one other article you wrote on the question of responsible journalism, which is separate from your outbursts against Islam?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We still have February 3, 2003, "Islam as sedition."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be S412A.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to make it absolutely clear, Dr. Trifkovic, before we look at this article you're perfectly entitled to hold any views you like about this tribunal but I want to ask you the basis for these views. There is no date on this article but in fact it appears on the list of your articles from the web site and it's dated March 2000. And it's headed "The Hague Tribunal, Bad Justice, Worse Politics." You deal with the detention unit at Scheveningen which you describe as ten miles away from the court. It is a small point but what makes you assert that it's ten miles away?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: First of all the correction about the date. This appeared in the Chronicles magazine in the June issue of 1996. Why it appears under the 2000 date line in -- on the web site, I do not know. I haven't looked at the web site version of it. Of course I remember the article well from the time when it appeared.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: The ten miles --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can show you your web site --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you. I'm saying simply that if we look at Chronicles magazine issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. This can't be correct that it's June issue of 1996, when you are quoting Toronto Star from November 3, 1992 -- 1999, on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that must be right because there is a reference we'll see later to Tadic being four years before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No that was -- in that case, something is mixed up here because the article under this heading was published in Chronicles of 1996. There was a subsequent article which was entitled something different, what the web site editor did with the two I do not know. I would need to read this article by itself, but please proceed with specific questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm perfectly happy, Dr. Trifkovic if you want to take time just to read through it. I don't want to take you by surprise on this. Do you want time to read through it?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: No, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The question I asked, was what made you assert that the court was ten miles from the detention unit? What did you base that on?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: That obviously is a mistake. I have no recollection of the ten mile assertion. At that time I may have based it on a secondhand press articles which in this particular instance were obviously wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look, please, at the third paragraph which begins, "The tradition, that is to say the International Court of Justice tradition," which you referred to in the previous paragraph, "is now being destroyed by a pseudo legal impostor, the Yugoslav War Crimes Tribunal, which was inserted deliberately into The Hague to provide the pretender with a legal and cultural pedigree and at the same time to devalue the true legacy. It is as if Jimmy Swaggart set up shop in Rome, took a crash course in Latin and took to wearing a Miter." For those who may not know, am I right in saying that Jimmy Swaggart was the television evangelist who actually fell foul of the law?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "It has funds --" I'm sorry, "This so-called Tribunal uses legal language. It has jurists on its panels and they are dressed in a bizarre imitation of continental judicial attire. It has funds, lots of funds, but it is a fraud." Is that a view you hold today?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: This is verbatim section from the article published in June of 1996, and I readily admit that I have considerably modified my views of the Tribunal in the intervening seven years.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's go on to the part that's headed, "Myth of the Bosnian Holocaust." And if we go over the page, please, to the third paragraph, which begins, "Kenny and others have proven that the Bosnian Holocaust story was fabricated by the Muslim side as part of a wide-ranging and effective PR campaign and eagerly embraced by their sympathisers in the media. In fact, after an initial bout of heavy fighting from 1993 to 1995, there was a period of relative calm on most fronts in Bosnia, interrupted by brief outbursts in isolated localities such as Gorazde and Bihac. Stories of mass murder and atrocities have not been substantiated even after sustained and well-publicised digs in the area of Srebrenica. Had there been a slaughter on the alleged scale, there would have been fewer rather than more voters especially on the Muslim side on the electoral roll in 1996 than in 1990." Now, first of all, is it still your view that, as you put it, the Bosnian Holocaust story was fabricated by the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: I greatly object to the use of the term "Holocaust" in the context of Bosnia because I still believe that it devalues the magnitude and the tragic tragedy of the Holocaust, which is the extermination of the European Jews by the Nazis during World War II. I still believe that even though it may be poor form to count the bodies, that the magnitude of the Bosnian war of 1992 to 1995 does not exceed in purely quantitative terms of victims and suffering a number of civil wars seen elsewhere around the world, including Spanish civil war of 1936 to 1939, including the Russian civil war during the revolution of 1917 to 21. To single out and I deliberately put in parenthesis Bosnian Holocaust as a defining moment which in terms of the number of victims and the magnitude of suffering is somehow unique and solely comparable to the Holocaust of 1942 to 1945 is misleading.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Stories of mass murder and atrocities not substantiated even after sustained and well-publicised digs in the area of Srebrenica." Are you saying that there was no massacre at Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not saying -- what I'm saying is on the form of the time when the article was written which I will need to look at my notes but this section of the article certainly refers to the period of the spring of 1996, there were many curious questions surrounding the Srebrenica episode, including the reappearance of a number of people who were claimed to have disappeared in Srebrenica in the ranks of the Muslim army. But what we have here is an obvious blending of two articles, one that deals with Bosnia and another one that deals with Kosovo over which I, frankly, did not have control. I am not saying that any of this is not written by me, I am simply putting it in the context that this looks like a somewhat clumsily put together melange of two different pieces.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. But why would somebody want to do that?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying that this was done -- if it -- it probably has to do with the dictates of the web site management deadlines which sometimes result in the print articles from the magazine being posted and articles that are related to a similar subject matter are sometimes bundled by the editor into single piece from two or three different articles by the same author without the author necessarily having a hand in the process of editing. I know it sounds complicated but this is the factual state.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you're going to be coming back tomorrow, Dr. Trifkovic, are you able overnight to get the two individual articles?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: I can try to do so, yes. We are looking at the article on -- from June of 1996 and then another one concerning the Kosovo. Yes, yes, I'll try to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You didn't actually answer the question. Do you now accept that there was a massacre of something in the region of 7.000 men and boys at Srebrenica by the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. If we leave out of -- we skip the next page, we come down to the real rationale at the bottom of page 3, where you deal again by saying there was no Holocaust and then say "So why the War Crimes Tribunal?" Mrs. Albright's answer and then you go on to quote what Madeleine Albright had to say and deal with American policy, which you end up by saying, "The Serbs were to be pilloried and the Tribunal was needed to give due legitimacy and pseudo legality to that decision." Was that part written in 1996 or in 2000?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: It was written in 1996 and it specifically referred to the U.S. intent behind the setting up of the Tribunal, as reflected in both Albright's statement and Susan Woodward's comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You then go on to say, "And pseudo legal it was" and so on and so forth, "The procedures --" I'm sorry, can you find that paragraph? That's three from the bottom -- "under which people are being tried at The Hague are outrageous, when the trial of Dusko Tadic was well underway four years ago, even The New York Times had to admit that the Court still needs to establish exactly what evidence will be admitted and what constitutes --" I think that should be "an offence." "The rules of evidence remain totally unclear to this day." Now, we can take it that part was written in 2000?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Also I will add that that part was based on my telephone interview with Alfred Rubin, Professor of International Law at Tufts University, with whom I had an extensive conversation concerning the evolving rules of evidence with trials under way and whose judgement I trusted on this issue, in view of his position as the chairman of the International Law Society of the United States.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. So you're saying that assertion, "The rules of evidence remain totally unclear to this day," is -- refers to a phone conversation you had with someone called Professor Rubin who said that rules were still evolving?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why didn't you say that in the article?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: I started quoting Professor Rubin higher up in the article, and as we proceeded, it is implied that what comes in cursive or parenthesis refers to other people's opinion. What you will find is that very often rather than repeat so and so says, quotes are put in either italics or parenthesis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in your view, as a historian, academic, political scientist, unclear means the same as evolving, does it?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not, and I would say that you can have perfect clarity about the process of evolution or else that you can have lack of clarity even if evolution is complete. What I would say, however, is that it would have been greatly preferable if the evolution had not continued while trials were underway.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But that's not what you say, is it?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That is not what you say in this article. You make a bald assertion that "The rules of evidence remain totally unclear to this day." And isn't that because you wanted your readers, whoever they may be, to believe that this was an unfair court?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: It is up to the reader to conclude whether the fairness is contained within the judicial process that continues to establish the rules of evidence even as trials are underway. I would simply submit, and now I quote from memory, Professor Rubin, "That it would be most remarkable for the domestic jurisdiction of any democratic country in the world to proceed on the similar basis." In other words, to change the rules of evidence while trials are already in process.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you're not a lawyer, Professor Trifkovic, it may be an unfair question. Have you never heard of a change in the laws while a trial is continuing?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, even though I'm not a lawyer, I believe it would be very difficult to retroactively affect the rights of the accused on the basis of evolving legislation that is enacted after the beginning of a person's trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we go to the next sentence, please? "Equally unacceptable in a normal court of law is that the fact that the accused has no right to confront his accuser. That means the accusers may remain anonymous. And as the American Bar Association has noted in a critique, immune from cross-examination." On what did you base that assertion?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of a paper published by the American Bar Association at the end of 1995, early 1996, and that -- the exact title and format of which I would have to check if I have access to the Internet, but it was certainly not my own extrapolation. It was a quoted opinion from the ABA.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "In short, contrary to any civilised system of justice, the accused is held guilty until proven innocent." On what did you base that?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: That again is the continuing -- whatever is in italics or parentheses is taken as a quote from a stated source rather than my own words.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So we are talking again about the American Bar Association?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: The ABA article which I will have to try and reference for you for the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was this written in 1996 or in 2000?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: It was definitely early on. It was written in the aftermath of -- it was -- it was in the very early days, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we go to the next page, please? The paragraph beginning "In contrast." "In contrast, by all accounts, The Hague Tribunal is a well-financed, well-oiled, sophisticated affair. Their witnesses are given red-carpet treatment at The Hague and a great deal of resources are brought to bear. A lot of time goes into preparing each case. Disregarding rules of evidence and established legal procedure, it investigates, indicts, prosecutes and renders sentence as a single body. Pausing there, when was that written?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And on what was that based?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it still troubles some legal minds, and I could quote a number of interlocutors that I have consulted in addition to professor Rubin in preparing this article that there has been no separation between the initiation of investigations, the trial itself, and the appeals procedure, that indeed to some it is extremely troubling that it is under the roof of a single institution that we have the initiation of investigations, the conduct on investigations itself, the indictment, the trial and the appeal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "The witnesses are given red-carpet treatment at The Hague." Now, where did you get that from?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: It related to the well-publicised facts at that time that those who want to come forward as Prosecution witnesses will be given not only immunity but, in case of well-founded fear of Prosecution in the country of origin, even new identity and a new life in the West, which considering the state of the collapsed societies of better part of former Yugoslavia in the aftermath of the wars, was a very alluring prospects for many.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: A well publicised fact. Can you actually please quote an article, a book, an interview, on which you based this.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: At the time of the Tadic trial, there were in fact articles both which again I, given the time and resources, will be able to reference. In both the Bosnian Muslim press and in the Belgrade press, in one case complementary to the Tribunal, in another case critical of the Tribunal, regarding the care and attention given to Prosecution witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. It demands that arbitrarily proclaimed war criminals be physically delivered to The Hague. What do you mean by arbitrarily proclaimed?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: No, "proclaimed" is a bad choice of word. "Arbitrarily accused" would be a better choice of words. And on balance, I believe that this Tribunal has been less selective in its choice of the accused recently than was the case back in 1996. I think that even a very objective observer looking at the roll call of the accused in 1996 would notice an ethnic imbalance that is glaring compared to the magnitude of atrocities and serious crimes committed on different sides of the divide or, rather, should be used the plural, of ethnic divides. I still believe that it is somewhat problematic that in the case of the Serbs, the responsibility extends all the way to the top of the command and control structure, both political and military, whereas Franjo Tudjman was allowed to die peacefully in his bed and Alija Izetbegovic is enjoying his twilight years as a retired head of state. I believe that an impartial and objective observer looking at the events of 1990 to 1992 would conclude that there is at least prima facie case for at least investigating and openly investigating, if not necessarily indicting, the political leaders of all three ethnic groups and that command and control responsibility in the case of the non-Serbs was somewhat arbitrarily cut somewhere halfway or two-thirds up the command and control ladder.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you aware, Dr. Trifkovic, that the issuing of an indictment has to be based upon evidence?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed I am, and that's why I'm saying that it is somewhat surprising that evidence such as there is or could have been established in the case of the two aforementioned leaders, has not been deemed sufficient for the Office of the Prosecutor to instigate proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's just finish off this paragraph. "It is not allowed defence attorneys to challenge the accusations by hiding itself behind a lack of mandate for trial in absentia. It has turned the NATO troops in the Balkans into its private gendarmerie empowered to hunt and arrest anyone it regards as a suspect. It is sustaining a world-wide media frenzy through which the accused are pronounced guilty by association and without a trial. It is destroying and making a mockery of the judicial system and secular legal tradition. The Hague story, besides being a travesty of the due process, as we know it, amounts to the abandonment of positive international law." Would you agree that this is a polemic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes it was written as a polemic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would you state that this is responsible journalism?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: If we postulate polemic as a rhetorical device that has specific purpose of putting controversial issues in sharp focus, I would say that this is as responsible as any number of op-eds or editorials that not only deal with the analysis of issues but with contentious opinions and with different scenarios for their long-term resolution. My cutting edge of the rhetorical turn of phrase, if you will, was particularly aimed not so much at The Hague Tribunal's procedures but as the longer term issue of the International Criminal Court, which I deal in the subsequent paragraph. Also let me add that at the time that these words being written in the spring of 1996 when we still had the era of Cherif Bassiouni's report as the initial body of evidence, later I understand discarded, and with Judge Goldstone's somewhat clumsy beginning of indictments that were sometimes surprising in their arbitrariness, I, being very frank, as I've been all day today, readily concede that from a distance of six or seven years I would have to end this rhetoric to a considerable extent today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the next paragraph, the one that begins, "There are people in Washington who have a different scenario in mind. They do not seek to delegitimise war crimes per se but to enhance their power to decide what is a war crime on the basis of current political calculations. Applied in recent practice, political discretion over what constitutes a war crime means that when Bosnian Muslims are shelled, driven from their homes, or murdered, those powerful Washingtonians are seething with indignation and they duly send The Hague into top gear, indict first, ask questions later. When Serbs are driven from their homes in the Krajina in 1995, or in Sarajevo in the winter of 1996, or from Kosovo to this very day, when they are expelled in their hundreds of thousands or are discovered with their throats cut, they pretend not to see." Now, first, we can take it from that that this paragraph was written in 2000?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: This paragraph was written in 2000, but very importantly it was written with reference to the outgoing Clinton administration, which was still very much in power at that time, and not with reference to the Bush administration, which is inaugurated about a year later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Am I right this paragraph is intended to suggest that this Tribunal is driven entirely by American policy?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: No. This paragraph seeks to suggest that there are elements in the American power structure as it was then, under President Clinton, and I was alluding specifically to the then-Secretary of State, Albright, who wanted to use the Tribunal for an arbitrary apportioning of guilt, or rather, to an arbitrary closing of the eyes to prima facie crimes against humanity committed by other sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, what is the sentence "they duly send The Hague into top gear, indict first, ask questions later," what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Well, "they" refers to the intelligence services of the major powers, in this particular case the United States, who supply the raw material, if you will, the primary body of evidence, that the Tribunal then turns into investigations and indictments.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In the next paragraph you return to your Islamic furrow, if that's the right word. "In the meantime, he who pays the piper calls the tune." At its inception The Hague Tribunal received 93.4 per cent of its funding from two Islamic countries, Pakistan and Malaysia." And where did you get that piece of information?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, that was stated -- and I'm now speaking from memory, I don't think -- because this is a compilation, it doesn't have the footnotes, but in the original there would have been a footnote. I believe this to have been stated by Cherif Bassiouni in an interview with the Chicago Tribune on the occasion of the publication of his initial report. I seem to recall that the figure of 93.4 per cent for the initial injection of financial liquidity was actually stated by Bassiouni himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mirabile --

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, let me add that I believe this was done in a complimentary sense that he was trying to point out how these countries were going beyond the call of duty to provide initial funding.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then of course, you turn it round the other way because you go on to say, "Mirabile dictu both have been given the right to appoint judges to the panel," so the suggestion there is because they gave the money, they got the judges; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: The suggestion is obvious because there are 150-odd member countries of the United Nations and if we have two, that provide the initial funding, and both are given seats on the initial panel, until proven otherwise, I think one is well justified to at least suspect prima facie linkage.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Speculation?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Speculation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. If we go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you also to provide this, it's not quoted here, it's not in italics but you're making reference to Professor Cherif Bassiouni about this 93.5 per cent of its funding from two Islamic countries, Pakistan and Malaysia, I would appreciate to get this source. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go over the page, please? "Many transgressors, par excellence. Are safe from Prosecution. The Bosnian Muslim government has stage-managed three well-publicised explosions in Sarajevo, in May, 1992, February, 1994, and August 1995. A total of 121 civilians has been killed as a result." On what did you base that allegation?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Satish Nambiar and -- well, Generals Nambiar and MacKenzie vis-a-vis the bread que massacre of May 1992. Lord David Owen's Balkan Odyssey refers to the Markale incident of February, 1994 in his memoirs. He mentioned in passing the existence of the secret UN report, and the way in which he used even the implied threat of its publication as a means of getting the Muslims to continue negotiating on -- at a time when -- I find it a little difficult to give you specific references to something that I wasn't preparing myself to comment upon in detail today. But let me say that for the Markale incident, from February of 1994, the press references to the existence of the secret UN report which establishes the impossibility of a single 120 millimetre mortar causing 80 deaths and considerably greater number of wounded in that particular location, have been made by, among others, the Daily Telegraph and the Independent. They have been specifically stated by a Russian colonel who was present with one of the two Russian battalions in the area, and whereas we can only conclude from circumstantial evidence that the report does exist, reference to it is made by both Sir Michael Rose in his memoirs and by, as I mentioned earlier, David Owen in his Balkan Odyssey.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So your sources for this are all books published by people who were, if I can put it that way, around at the time?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You have never looked at any of the evidence relating to the actual investigations that were carried out?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the problem with that is that it appears to have been the case that we had two different sets of investigations, and that some of them were made public and others were not. For instance, there is again in both Nambiar's and McKenzie's accounts, a specific reference to the Vase Miskina Street being cordoned off some minutes before the bread queue explosion and a video camera making an appearance in situ. There is also the reference in Sir Michael Rose and in David Owen, to the existence of this secret UN report, which both emphasise had been progressively reduced in the number of persons that were allowed access to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, Dr. Trifkovic, the point is this: Don't you see any problem at all as a historian, political scientist, journalist, in asserting as a fact "The Bosnian Muslim government has stage-managed three well-publicised explosions" without qualifying that in any way?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: The best qualification that I can give to these events is cui bono. If we have time after time outrages in the Balkans that are almost automatically, almost reflexively, ascribed to one particular side of the conflict, and if we have reasonable doubt on that interpretation of the events, given by some of the highest officials of the international community on the ground, be they military or political personalities, I think that reasonable doubt that you mention should be on the other side, on the side that has almost reflexively, I emphasise, blamed the Serb side for each and every of those events.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You didn't even think of perhaps using an expression like the "evidence suggests"?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: I admit that it would have been more prudent for me to have done so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And finally, on this article, if we look at the penultimate paragraph on page 6, "It could hardly be otherwise," you're referring back to the Prosecutions, "since the model for The Hague Tribunal is not Nuremberg 1946 but Moscow 1938. It is a deeply flawed institution created for dishonest political ends. It is also an obscene travesty of justice as understood and practice in the civilised world." Written in 1996 or 2000?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You don't think that the way you put that is extreme?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Extremism is in the eye of the beholder. In 1996, if we look at again I submit the list of the accused, if we look at the initial brief, if we look at the behaviour of the first Prosecutor and his public statements, if we look at the initial report Cherif Bassiouni's report that provide the initial body of evidence, it was a politicised body par excellence, I have already mentioned and I will mention it again, that from seven years distance, I would rephrase some of these statements quite considerably so, and that without, in any event, trying to justify Trifkovic, 1996, I would say that Trifkovic 2003 would seek a more fortuitous formulation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Dr. Trifkovic, isn't it in fact the case that far from being an objective observer of these events and their aftermath, you are in fact a strongly committed Serb nationalist?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: It is interesting that views that are shared by a large number of non-Serbs, whether they be political or legal commentators, are in this case equated with, as you put it, Serbian nationalism. Since I'm not a lawyer, I am not sure what would be the legal definition of a nationalist but I would say that for each and every element in my statements, especially as they relate to the period and the context in which they were expressed, I could quote a number of authors who have neither ethnic or emotional connection with the Balkans, and who have expressed similar opinions and similar sentiments. Furthermore, I would say that the same phenomenon applies to the other side, to people who are sympathetic to the Bosnian Muslims, for instance. One of them, Ed Vulliamy was accepted as an expert witness even though, in one of his interviews with the Bosnian press, he openly referred to Serb civilians, all Serb civilians, as Chetniks and in the context of Serb civilians leaving Sarajevo in the winter of 1996 said it was the right and proper thing for them to go because they condoned aggression. It is quite possible that in the study of these emotionally-laden and extremely controversial issues, people take strong opinions and sides and argue their cases both analytically and polemically. You have chosen to focus on some of my articles which are written quite openly in the spirit of polemics, but at the same time I would submit that in the polemical spirit, you will find many other prominent analysts of that part of the world, such as Robert Fisk, such as Christiane Amanpour, saying or asserting things that, from the distance of four, five, six or seven years, they would prefer to have stated differently and whose not only analysis but even more pertinently running commentary on current events have not withstood the test of time. For what it's worth, I will say that had I still retained my jaundiced view of the proceedings in this Court that I held in the spring of 1996, I would not have agreed to appear as expert witness, and that it is exactly because I believe that with a change of both personnel and modus operandi, it is, if not ideal, certainly the only available and therefore the best show in town to ascertain who did what to whom in the Balkans, how and why, that I am here today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is the answer to my question, Dr. Trifkovic, no, you are not a Serb nationalist?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who told you, Dr. Trifkovic, that Mr. Vulliamy was an expert witness?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Reference to that was made in the article in one of the Bosnian Muslim papers, which again I didn't regard it as significant. I didn't bring it with me and I didn't mention it in the -- in the -- in my analysis, but it was an interview I think prompted by the fact that he was engaged as an expert witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who told you that he was engaged as an expert witness?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: No one told me. I'm saying in the article, in which there is an interview with Vulliamy, in one of the Bosnian Muslim papers, there is -- the reference is made to Vulliamy's testimony in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you this next, please: Did you read any of the testimony that has been given in this case before writing your report, or after?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: The only testimony I did read was the military report -- sorry, the testimony of the military witness Ewan Brown.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And why did you read Mr. Brown's testimony?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: It was given to me by Mr. Ostojic in late November. It was the only bundle of -- it was the only actual piece of testimony that I was given.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you weren't given the testimony of a Mr. Semenovic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not given the testimony of Mr. Semenovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Or any of the testimony of Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was only given the two written documents by Dr. Donia, the short and the long one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So the short one that you described being Dr. Donia's report headed, "Prijedor in the Bosnian Krajina, a background report"?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the long one that you have referred to is, "The Bosnian Krajina in the history of Bosnia and Herzegovina"?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in effect, your report is a response largely to his big report; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: It may have started as a response to that and evolved into an attempt to present a broad-picture context of the Prijedor events. In other words, whereas the initial impetus was to write a response to Donia's long report, in the end it evolved into an attempt to tell a story by itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because when we look at your report, there is very little that is actually concerned with Prijedor itself; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think everything is concerned with Prijedor itself because I don't believe that anything that has taken place in Prijedor would have taken place were it not for broader events taking place outside of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that. You make that clear in your report. But the actual consideration of events in Prijedor, by my count, amounts to some four, seven, nine pages.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that is about right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As a matter of interest, did you ask why you were being given Ewan Brown's report, which was a military analysis, rather than any other documents?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Because the initial possibility that Mr. Ostojic had mentioned was that I would also refer to the military aspects of the problem, but having looked at the material, I concluded that in this area, I would indeed be out of my depth and that I preferred not to deal with issues that would fall outside my area of expertise and close personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, because you have no expertise, as I understand it, in military history.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I do have a lot of expertise in military history, but not in ongoing or very recent military history of Bosnia in 1991-2.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to come to the report itself and some of the assertions that you make. Before I do that, are you able to say which of the documents, the newspaper articles and the books you saw before writing the report and which only after? Do you have a list?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you have a list?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Of?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The documents you saw before you wrote the report and those you saw after the report had been delivered.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. What you have in the footnotes of the report are the documents that I've seen prior to delivering the report. We have to assume, and I think it is correct to say, that whatever is not listed in the footnotes has been given to me subsequent to the report's submission.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And were those footnotes written by you as well?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, then, can we look, please at the -- have you got your report there in front of you? Dr. Trifkovic, do you have the report?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You do, all right. Can we look, please, first of all, then, at the second page? And it's a small point but I'd just like to ask you. It's under the heading, "Eastern question and Europe," where you have a footnote relating to your sentence that the unprecedented propagandistic depiction of Turkey as tolerant and humane, and the myth lingers on even today in some quarters," and you footnote there that such bias is notably present in Noel Malcolm's, "Bosnia, a short history." And It's right, isn't it, that you refer to him a number of occasions, nearly always critically?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to the issue of the character of the Ottoman Empire, I think that Noel Malcolm's overall treatment of the subject matter would definitely fall into the category of apologetics.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's more the next sentence that I want to ask you about: "The true record is nevertheless clear and it was aptly summarised in a British diplomat's report from Turkey in 1909," and you quote. Which diplomat and where do we find that?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. It is the British consul general in Mosul, in today's northern Iraq, and he referred specifically to the question posed by the Foreign Office as to what was the effect of the young Turks' putative reforms on the position of religious minorities on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Actually, the real question - I'm sorry, I phrased it rather badly - is why didn't you footnote that when you wrote it?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: I admit I should have done so. I assure you that the quote is genuine and it is contained in a number of sources. It is the British consul general in Mosul.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we go then, please, now, to page 7, which is headed, "World War II bloodbath"? And in the third paragraph, you state, "The technique of Ustasha killing was savage. A slit throat or a blow with a heavy club in the back of the head was the most common method." The first thing I want to know is why you felt it necessary to describe this in your report?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Because the whole trauma of the Ustasha experience, both in Prijedor itself and in the context of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole, must not be underestimated when we try to understand the frame of mind and the collective psychosis of the different ethnic groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the outset of the conflict in 1991-92.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I stop you there? I understand why you've included what happened in the 1941 period onwards but why was it necessary to describe in this sort of gory detail the method of killing?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, by the way, the specific description of the savagery, and this is again something that is only indirectly apparent from my references at the bottom of the page, is that the Axis commanders on the ground were making comments about this, and expressing shock and outrage. Italian commanders, I could quote names, Ambrosio, in the case of the Germans, Glaise von Horstenau, and his assistant, captain whose name now escapes me, in other words, what I am doing here is not so much give my own description out of the blue but putting things in the context, because what happened in Prijedor on the night of August 3rd, 4th of 1941 is something that has been commented upon by the German field commanders and not only by the historians of the war on the Partizan side, i.e., on the winning side, in -- after 1945.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I ask -- as I understand it, you're saying that's why you describe it as the most common method because two people described it?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: No. The description is actually well established through countless commissions that explored the mass graves all over the so-called independent state of Croatia in the after math of 1945. In fact the Ustashas made a public point of saying that they would not waste bullets and the -- the aforementioned methods of killing, for instance, were amply present in the entire area of the Jasenovac concentration camps which again is a matter well established, well documented, and I didn't deem it necessary to make particular reference to it because it's not even denied by anyone of repute.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I will simply return to my original question: Why did you feel it necessary to include in this report a description of how the killings happened?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: Because on the night of August 3rd, 4th of 1941, that was the method of the killing used by the Ustasha Flying Gendarmerie in the city of Prijedor. The consequences of that night of terror were commented upon in, again, even more graphic detail than I did, by the Commission for the Establishment of Crimes of Occupiers and their Collaborators of the Peoples Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the late 1940s, as well as by the report of the Wehrmacht field commander who came to relieve the city of Prijedor and who sent to Glaise von Horstenau in Zagreb a report expressing his outrage at the savagery that he witnessed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we move on, please? Page 8. At the bottom of that page, you say this: "In fact, until 1945, more Bosnian Muslims fought in German uniform notably in the 7th SS Hanjar Sword Division than as partisans. What is your source of that assertion?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the numbers of members of the veterans --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want the source, please, I'm sorry, Dr. Trifkovic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [resumed]
